title: Chapter 18 — That Amongst The Americans All Honest Callings Are Honorable
paragraphs: Among a democratic people, where there is no inherited wealth, every man either works for a living, has worked, or is born of parents who have worked. The idea of labor is therefore presented to the mind on every side as the necessary, natural, and honest condition of human existence. Not only is labor not dishonorable among such a people; it is held in honor. The prejudice is not against it, but in its favor. In the United States a wealthy man thinks he owes it to public opinion to devote his leisure to some kind of industrial or commercial pursuit, or to public affairs. He would think himself in bad standing if he spent his life solely on living. It is to escape this obligation to work that so many rich Americans come to Europe, where they find scattered remains of aristocratic society among which idleness is still honored.

Equality of conditions not only ennobles the idea of labor in men's eyes; it raises the idea of labor undertaken for profit. In aristocracies it is not exactly labor that is scorned, but labor pursued for gain. Labor is honorable in itself when undertaken at the sole command of ambition or virtue. Yet in aristocratic society it constantly happens that a man who works for honor is not indifferent to the attractions of profit. These two desires mingle only in the innermost depths of his soul. He carefully hides from every eye the point at which they meet; he would like to hide it even from himself. In aristocratic countries there are few public officials who do not claim to serve their country without self-interested motives. Their salary is a detail they think little about, and always pretend not to think about at all. In this way the notion of profit is kept separate from the notion of labor. However closely the two may be joined in fact, they are not thought of together.

In democratic communities, by contrast, these two notions are always openly united. Since the desire for well-being is universal, since fortunes are modest or fluctuating, since everyone wants either to increase his own resources or to provide new ones for his children, men see clearly that it is profit which — if not entirely, at least partly — leads them to work. Even those chiefly driven by the love of fame are necessarily brought to the thought that fame is not their only motive. They discover that the desire to earn a living is mixed in their minds with the desire to make life distinguished.

As soon as, on the one hand, labor is regarded by the whole community as an honorable necessity of man's condition, and, on the other, as soon as labor is always openly performed wholly or in part for the sake of earning remuneration, the immense gap that once separated the various callings in aristocratic societies disappears. If all are not alike, all at least have one feature in common. No profession exists in which men do not work for money, and the remuneration common to all gives them all a kind of family resemblance. This helps explain the opinions Americans hold about different callings. In America no one is degraded because he works, for everyone around him also works; nor is anyone humiliated by the thought of receiving pay, for the President of the United States also works for pay. He is paid for commanding, other men for obeying orders. In the United States professions are more or less laborious, more or less profitable, but they are never high or low: every honest calling is honorable.
